opeds.headline: Don't Put a Federal Permit on Open AI
opeds.subtitle: A Senate markup would ration the future Meta says is for everyone.
opeds.body:
Next Wednesday, Senate Commerce is scheduled to mark up a bill that would require a federal license before any lab can release a capable AI model that the public can download, run, and modify. The same week, Meta is running a campaign under a title that does not hedge: The Future Is for Everyone.

Those two facts cannot survive contact with each other.

A license desk does not produce a future for everyone. It produces a future for the firms that can staff the eighteen-month wait, the compute audit, and the outside counsel. Everyone else rents access on the licensed labs' terms.

Congress should kill the pre-release licensing approach. Police the place where private lives actually get fused — the data-broker layer sitting in this country. Require any company that puts an AI system into a role that already carries legal duties to post real capital against real damage. Put a clock and a published test on every restriction, and repeal it automatically if the test fails. That is how you get safety without building a cartel.

History is not subtle on this point. Every serious jump in human welfare came from people trying things without a ministry's permission. The printing press. Grid electricity. Open-source software. Linux did not wait for a federal operating-system license. The web did not wait for a content permit. Those systems produced mess. They also produced the reason you are reading this on a device that would have been a supercomputer a generation ago.

Freeze the next general-purpose technology behind a licensing window and you are not buying caution. You are buying three labs, two cloud vendors, and one set of terms. That is a moat. Call it what it is.

Now scale the cost. Drug-discovery cycles that stay locked inside a licensed lab. A diagnostic model that never reaches a county hospital because the files cannot be posted. A closed-loop insulin system a clinic could have adapted from a public model, sitting in a queue while a committee debates a hypothetical. When you choose to freeze development out of imagined catastrophe, you are choosing to let people die today of diseases we could automate a cure for. Who gave you the right to make that choice for them?

The wins that already exist showed up in the field, not in white papers. Protein-folding tools in the hands of working biologists. Imaging readers in clinics. Warehouse labor coming off broken backs and onto software. What a system does after it ships beats a whiteboard scenario every time. Hill offices are trained to price the risk of shipping. They are not trained to price the people abundance never reached.

And it gets worse when the bill aims at the wrong door. AI harm does not arrive as a priced sale of a model file. It arrives when a broker aggregates what you already handed over. It arrives when a buyer joins two separately clean files and rebuilds a person. It arrives when a trained model memorizes a life that a notify-on-sale rule never sees. A transaction trigger has no firing event for that. You cannot license your way around it.

The systems themselves will not sit still for a paper review. An AI model's behavior is inseparable from the hospital, the school, the claims desk that wraps it. Outcomes cannot be predicted from the files alone, and they cannot be blamed on the files alone. A pre-release license application is a ritual. It is not a measurement.

The chokepoint that actually sits still is the aggregator in this jurisdiction, and the act of deploying into a real institution. Police those. Leave the public files alone.

Fine — public models can be pointed at ugly targets. A coding model can write malware. A literature model can be aimed badly. That is real. So fix it with capital and evidence, not with a gate. Any entity that deploys AI into credit, medicine, hiring, or custody should hold an uncapped backstop against the damage it can cause, with a named officer whose personal liability cannot be written down to zero. Watch the system after it ships. If a restriction cannot show, against numbers you published in advance, that it cut harm inside a fixed window, it dies. No renewal hearing. No permanent emergency.

That is insurance. Licensing is a queue that protects whoever already cleared it.

Senate Commerce can still rewrite the markup before it leaves the room. Three instructions would do the work.

Tell the Federal Trade Commission and the state attorneys general to go after privacy harm at the broker-aggregation layer, tied to the in-country deployment, not to a sale that never happens when the harm lives inside a trained model.

Tell Treasury and the banking regulators to condition legal duty-bearing status for a deployed AI system on a required capital floor structured as an uncapped backstop, attached to a named officer.

Tell the White House science office and the federal standards agency that every restriction they write gets a clock and a metric. Miss the metric, the rule expires.

Meta's campaign has the destination right and is too polite about the obstacle. The future is for everyone only if public models stay legal to release, fork, and run. People will use those tools to change how they work, how they learn, and — when the science is ready — how they modify their own biology and minds. That is not a side effect. That is the point.

Next Wednesday the committee can choose a license window or a country that still ships. The patient, the shop-floor tech, and the kid who would have built on a public model will not be in the room. They will live with the choice. Who gave you the right to make it for them?

opeds.headline: Meta’s Future Needs a Kill Switch Congress Can Pull
opeds.subtitle: A slogan is not a rollback plan — and no one at the company has named who can halt the systems.
opeds.body:
Meta is circulating a manifesto on the Hill this month — “The Future is for Everyone” — as Senate Commerce prepares to mark up the first AI accountability bill of the session. The page is bright. The ask is simple. Put the systems in as many hands as possible, treat them as a public good, and write the law as if distribution were the safeguard.

Lawmakers are being invited to treat that vision as the default. It is not a default. It is a request to lift the last boundary we still hold over machines we cannot fully inspect, cannot fully predict, and cannot fully recall once they run at population scale.

Human control is not a feature to bolt on after launch. It is the condition under which any future remains ours to correct. Congress should refuse legal permission, safe harbor, or federal procurement for large-scale AI until the deployer can name the humans who can halt it, the criteria that force a halt, and the liability that follows if they do not.

We spent centuries building the institutional guardrails that keep society stable. On what authority does a company claim we can remove them because the product is popular?

The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer. The software that pushed those noses down was not a riddle of physics. It was a failure of who held the authority to say no, and of who would answer when the system did something its builders had not advertised. Aviation recovered because the grounding order still sat in human hands, and because the public could name the agency that used it.

Markets learned a related lesson in 2008. Instruments no single desk fully understood were joined across institutions until the join itself became the risk. No ingestion check at any one bank saw the mosaic. The harm formed downstream, at a fusion no gate observed. Capital rules and resolution authority were rebuilt not out of hostility to finance, but because complex human systems require boundaries to survive. Removing those boundaries systematically triggers collapse.

Meta’s manifesto asks the country to distribute the next generation of models first and govern them later. The company’s own record is a study in sociotechnical complexity: outcomes that cannot be read from the code alone or from the terms of service alone. A ranking system, a recommendation engine, a generative model — each behaves as it does because of the institution around it, the incentives inside it, and the people it trains on. When those systems fail, attribution dissolves. That is not a reason to wait for perfect knowledge. It is a reason to keep a human hand on the halt.

We cannot fully verify a model’s goals. We cannot predict its behavior when the world shifts underneath the data it was trained on. We cannot encode moral discernment as a loss function. The human heart is not a compute problem. Emotional judgment, historical memory, and the capacity to refuse are not bugs in the deployment plan. They are the last uncomputable check we have — the same check we still grant a soldier who will not fire even when the law permits it.

Re-identification harm forms the same way the 2008 join did. Two datasets, each lawfully collected, each clean at the gate, produce a named person when they meet downstream. Meta holds more of those datasets than any private actor on earth. Open-weight models trained on that world, or fine-tuned against it, do not come with a transaction trigger that notices the mosaic. Models calibrated to the same privacy promise leak differently. No statute requires anyone to report the difference.

The case for wide access is not empty. Researchers use open models to study disease. Small firms reach tools they could not otherwise touch. A slower path has costs, and concentrating the off switch creates failure modes of its own — capture by the state, lock-in by whoever already sits at the table. Those risks are real.

They are not an argument for having no switch at all. The positive outcomes are real — and that is exactly why governance has to ensure they continue. Ungoverned success is luck, not safety. Precaution is the asymmetry between a mistake you can reverse and a deployment you cannot call back. Speed is not a virtue when the failure is unrecoverable.

Senate Commerce should write dual kill criteria into the markup: a customer-side validation failure that forces a halt, and a separate third-party harm channel with its own intake and a fiduciary duty to report upward. The two triggers must not share a desk. The Federal Trade Commission should treat the absence of a named rollback authority as an unfair practice for any model released at population scale. The National Institute of Standards and Technology should require deployers to publish how differently models leak when they claim the same privacy budget — a measurement, not a press release.

Meta’s board can act without waiting for a statute. Name the officers who hold halt authority. Publish the chain. State what evidence trips it. Tell the Commerce Committee, in writing, what the rollback plan is and who has the legal power to trigger it.

If the answer is that no such person exists, the manifesto has already answered the only question that matters. A future that cannot be stopped does not belong to everyone. It belongs to whoever shipped it. The committee marks up a bill this session. The grounding order is still available. After the systems are everywhere, it will not be.

*[Author] is a former federal technology regulator. The views expressed are their own.*

opeds.headline: Meta’s Future Isn’t for Everyone. Follow the Pipes.
opeds.subtitle: Congress should ignore the slogan and write three boring rules about data, liability, and the grid.
opeds.body:
This month Meta is flooding the Hill with a campaign called “The Future is for Everyone.” The site is bright and civic. Artificial intelligence, it says, will put tools once reserved for laboratories into the hands of teachers, shop owners, and kids.

The timing is not subtle. House Energy and Commerce staff are circulating a draft AI accountability bill. Senate Commerce has a markup window. Meta, in the same weeks, is asking Midwestern utilities for new power and water allotments to feed the next training clusters. The slogan arrived with the lobbyists.

That is not a public-interest campaign. It is a claim on the grid, on personal data, and on the hours people still have left in a day, dressed as access.

Lawmakers should stop arguing over whether this software will save civilization or end it. Write three enforceable rules instead: no training on personal information without consent, a named officer on the hook for every model release, and a clamp on the data-broker market that prices the rest of us before any chatbot opens its mouth.

Start with what the machine actually is. Not a mind. A warehouse.

Meta’s training clusters are buildings that drink electricity and water on a municipal scale. Towns in Iowa and Nebraska have already watched industrial users bid against households for the same aquifer and the same substation. The company books the productivity story in its shareholder letters. Ratepayers book the capacity charges on the monthly statement.

Translate that into a person. A shift supervisor in Council Bluffs does not get a vote on whether the next model run is “for everyone.” She gets a higher summer bill and a tenant that will be gone the day the tax abatement expires.

Who captures the financial windfall? The people who already own the compute, the model weights, and the ad exchange that monetizes whatever attention the new toys pull in. Dual-class stock keeps that answer from ever going to a real vote.

The campaign talks about tools. It does not talk about the feedstock.

Every “free” model is trained on other people’s writing, photos, messages, and faces. The little switches in Settings govern the last mile. They do not touch the market that already priced the linkage. Data brokers sell re-identification packages before any agent runs. Your name is already a row. The chatbot is the storefront.

This is the part both the boosters and the doom caucus keep skipping. Downstream gates — safety filters, watermarking, an “AI safety” team with a nice org chart — attach to the deployed product. The broker-aggregation layer sits upstream. That is where linkage is priced and sold. Mechanisms bolted onto the chatbot leave the chokepoint alone.

Attention is the other extraction. Meta’s business is not democratizing the future. It is metering how long you look. Shared attention — the thing that makes a town meeting or a newsroom or a family dinner work — gets broken into inventory and auctioned. Call that opportunity if you want. On the ground it looks like a feed engineered to keep the auction open.

None of this is an autonomous force arriving from the future. It is an infrastructure project. Semiconductors, substations, cooling loops, contract moderators, and a brokerage market in personal data. The outcomes cannot be read off the model card or the org chart alone. They come from the whole arrangement: who owns the pipes, who labels the toxic content for a few dollars an hour so the safety audit passes, who has no recourse when the ranking system decides what a teenager sees at 1 a.m.

When something goes wrong, the preferred fix is a solvency gadget. An insurance floor. A clawback clause. A departmental inbox. Those tools locate a payer after the harm. They do not create a duty of care before it.

A department cannot owe you a standard of care. A named human can. Every release should carry a signature on an enumerated hazard checklist — training-data provenance, known failure modes, supply-chain sources — and that signature should be the liability record. Not a press release. A name that still has a mortgage.

Section 230 was written for bulletin boards, not for firms that generate text and rank what billions of people see. Surgical amendments can restore accountability for the outputs a company produces and the ranking systems it runs, without burning down the statute’s core protections for users posting in their own voice. That is a drafting job for Commerce and Judiciary. It is not a seminar on machine souls.

The open-weights story will be the first objection, and it is not fake. Small shops do run Llama. A teacher in Ohio can put a tutor in front of a classroom without a Microsoft invoice. Download counts are real. Pretending otherwise is just a different sales pitch.

The uncomfortable part is what still sits upstream of those downloads. The same company that hands out the weights still owns the distribution, still scrapes the training corpus, still sells the ads around the resulting traffic, and still has no officer who will sit in a room when a school district or a clinic has to explain a failure. Free software on a captured pipeline is not a commons. It is a loss-leader.

Three actors. Three jobs.

Congress should move a narrow Section 230 fix that treats generated and ranked outputs as the company’s, not the user’s, and should require a named officer to sign a hazard checklist for each model release. No department letterhead. A person.

The Federal Trade Commission should treat the data-broker linkage market as the actual choke point — the place where privacy is priced and sold before any safety screen ever loads — and shut down the non-consensual trade in re-identification. Privacy is not a settings menu. It is a boundary.

State utility commissions should stop handing out water and power as if a slogan were a public-benefit finding. If Meta wants the grid, Meta posts the bond, publishes the draw, and pays the true cost of the substation.

The campaign site will keep saying the future is for everyone. Someone on the markup should ask the household drawing from the same aquifer who “everyone” did not include.
